The best options for cleaning Xcode’s `DerivedData` (and related bloat) range from dedicated developer apps to built-in macOS tools:

---

### 1. The Best Dedicated App: **DevCleaner for Xcode** (Free / Open Source)
**DevCleaner** is the gold standard among iOS and macOS developers. Unlike generic system cleaners, it is specifically designed to understand Xcode's directory structures.

* **Why it’s great:**
  * Categorizes clutter clearly: **DerivedData**, **Device Support** (often 20–50 GB alone), **Archives**, **Logs**, and **Documentation Caches**.
  * Lets you inspect individual projects and selectively delete old builds without wiping your active project.
  * Notifies you periodically when cache files grow past a threshold.
* **Where to get it:** Free on the [Mac App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/devcleaner-for-xcode/id1388020431) or via GitHub.

---

### 2. The Built-in Way: **macOS System Settings** (No Install Needed)
macOS has a dedicated developer storage manager:

1. Open **System Settings** > **General** > **Storage**.
2. Scroll to the **Developer** category and click the **(i)** info icon.
3. You can see exact breakdowns and click **Delete** on **Xcode Caches**, **Derived Data**, or **Device Support files** directly.

---

### 3. The Fastest Way: **Terminal Alias** (Power Users)
If you only care about `DerivedData` and want an instant, zero-overhead fix, adding an alias to your shell is the most efficient method:

1. Open `~/.zshrc` (or `~/.bashrc`):
   ```bash
   nano ~/.zshrc
   ```
2. Add this alias:
   ```bash
   alias cleandd="rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData"
   ```
3. Save and reload (`source ~/.zshrc`). Now typing `cleandd` wipes the entire directory instantly.

*(Bonus: To also purge orphaned simulator caches that hog storage, run:)*
```bash
xcrun simctl delete unavailable
```

---

### 4. The Best Menu/Launcher Tools:
* **Raycast (Xcode Extension):** If you use the Raycast launcher, search for the community-made **Xcode** extension. It allows you to wipe `DerivedData` or manage simulators with a single keystroke.
* **Eraser for Xcode:** A lightweight menu bar utility available on the Mac App Store that allows one-click DerivedData purges and scheduled cache cleanups.

---

### Summary Recommendation
* For a **visual breakdown and deep cleanup** (DerivedData + 30GB+ of old iOS symbols/simulators), use **DevCleaner for Xcode**.
* For **quick day-to-day DerivedData purges** when a build breaks, use a **Terminal alias** or **Raycast**.
* Avoid paid, general-purpose cleaners (like CleanMyMac) solely for Xcode files—they offer less granular control over developer caches than free dedicated tools.

To clear the media cache in Premiere Pro on a Mac, use the built-in setting. Deleting the files manually is the fallback.

**Method 1: Inside Premiere Pro (recommended)**
1. Quit any open Premiere Pro projects and the app itself. Then reopen Premiere Pro. A project doesn't need to be open; the Home screen works.
2. Open the settings menu. On macOS 13 and later, go to **Premiere Pro > Settings > Media Cache**. On older macOS versions, the item is under **Preferences**. On macOS, Preferences is under the Premiere Pro menu, not Edit.
3. Click **Delete...** next to the media cache files option. You'll see two choices:
   - **Delete unused media cache files** removes cache for source media that Premiere can no longer find.
   - **Delete all media cache files from the system** removes everything. Deleted cache files are recreated automatically whenever source media requires them.
4. Confirm. Premiere rebuilds the cache as you work, so expect some slowdown the next time you open footage.

**Method 2: Safe Mode-style reset (Premiere 2023 and later)**
Hold the Shift key while launching Premiere Pro, choose **Clear Media Cache Files**, and click Continue. Allow a few moments as Premiere Pro rebuilds the Media Cache.

**Method 3: Manually in Finder**
Quit all Adobe apps first. Then delete the contents of these folders (the Library folder is hidden; press Shift+Cmd+G in Finder and enter `~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/Common/`):
- Media Cache Files
- Media Cache

Deleting these with Premiere closed removes the current cache files as well, which is what you want when troubleshooting.

**Notes**
- Clearing the cache doesn't touch your project files or original footage. The cache is regenerated data.
- If you want to stop it from growing back, you can set a size or age limit in the same Media Cache settings panel, or move the cache location to an external drive. Keep in mind that the drive must be connected whenever you open Premiere.
- Adobe recommends clearing the cache after updating Premiere Pro or macOS.

There are three ways to clear the media cache in Adobe Premiere Pro on a Mac, depending on how thorough you want to be.

---

### Method 1: Inside Premiere Pro (Recommended)

To delete **all** media cache files (not just unused ones), you must close all open projects first.

1. Open Premiere Pro, but **do not open a project** (stay on the Home screen). If a project is open, go to **File > Close Project**.
2. In the top Apple menu bar, go to **Premiere Pro > Settings** *(or **Preferences** on older versions)* **> Media Cache**.
3. Look for the section labeled **Remove Media Cache Files** and click the **Delete** button.
4. Select **"Delete all media cache files from the system"** *(this option is only available if all projects are closed)*.
5. Click **OK**.

---

### Method 2: On App Startup (Reset Options)

This is the fastest method if you are running Premiere Pro 23.2 or newer:

1. Hold down the **Option** key on your keyboard while clicking the Premiere Pro app icon to launch it.
2. A **Reset Options** dialog box will appear.
3. Check the box for **"Clear media cache files"**.
4. Click **Continue**.

---

### Method 3: Manually via Finder (Deep Clean)

If Premiere Pro won't open, is crashing, or the buttons inside the app aren't freeing up storage space, you can delete the files directly from Finder:

1. **Quit Premiere Pro** completely (**Command + Q**).
2. Open **Finder**.
3. Press **Command + Shift + G** to open the "Go to Folder" prompt.
4. Paste the following path and press Return:
   ```text
   ~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/Common/
   ```
5. You will see several folders. Open and delete the contents inside:
   * **Media Cache**
   * **Media Cache Files**
   * **Peak Files** *(contains audio waveform data)*
6. **Empty your Mac's Trash** to actually reclaim the disk space.

---

### Pro Tip: Set Up Automatic Cache Management
To prevent cache files from taking up tens or hundreds of gigabytes in the future:
* Go back to **Premiere Pro > Settings > Media Cache**.
* Under **Media Cache Management**, choose:
  * **"Automatically delete cache files older than..."** (e.g., 30 or 60 days), or
  * **"Automatically delete oldest cache files when cache exceeds..."** (e.g., 50 GB).

Here are the most effective steps, starting with the biggest wins.

**1. Use Apple's built-in storage tools**
Go to **Apple menu > System Settings > General > Storage**. macOS lists categories by size and suggests fixes:
- **Empty the Trash.** Files you delete stay there and still take up space.
- **Optimize Storage.** This removes watched Apple TV shows and movies and, when storage is low, offloads photos and files to iCloud.
- **Store in iCloud** for Desktop and Documents. Only recently used files stay on your Mac.
- **Remove unused apps**, which you can review in the list.

**2. Find the biggest files yourself**
- Open **Finder**, then press **Cmd + F**, or use the Finder search bar.
- Click the "This Mac" dropdown and choose a search for file size, such as "File Size is Very Large" or "Greater Than 1 GB."
- Or open the Storage page and click the "i" next to a category (like Applications or Documents) to sort by size.

**3. Clear the common space hogs**
- **Downloads folder:** Installers (.dmg, .pkg) and old archives often sit here. Sort by size and delete what you don't need.
- **Old iPhone/iPad backups:** Go to Finder's sidebar, select the device, and check Backups. Or look in `~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup`.
- **Mail attachments:** In Mail, go to Mailbox > Erase Deleted Items, and check Mail's storage under Settings.
- **Messages attachments:** In Messages, go to Settings > iMessage and review "Keep Messages" (set it to 30 days or 1 year). Large attachments can be deleted from the conversation info view.
- **Xcode or developer tools:** Simulators and derived data can use tens of GB. Use `xcrun simctl delete unavailable` or delete them in Xcode settings.
- **Photos library:** Use Photos' "Duplicates" album and remove what you don't need.

**4. Clear caches (carefully)**
Caches rebuild automatically, so deleting them is safe. "System Data" in Storage often includes them. A restart can also clear some temporary files, and that sometimes frees a surprising amount of space.

**5. Consider external storage or cleanup tools**
- Move large media, old projects, and archives to an external drive.
- Third-party cleaners such as CleanMyMac or DaisyDisk can visualize disk usage. Be cautious with "free up RAM" or "optimizer" claims, which are often overstated. Only delete what you recognize.

**If the drive is almost completely full:** macOS needs some free space to run, so aim for at least 10 to 15 GB free. If you're stuck, start with the Storage page recommendations and the Downloads folder, since those usually recover the most space with the least risk.

When your Mac's storage is completely full, it can slow down significantly or prevent apps from opening. Here is a step-by-step guide to quickly reclaim several gigabytes of space:

---

### 1. Quick Wins (Immediate Space)

* **Empty your Trash:** Files aren’t deleted until you empty the Trash. Right-click the **Trash** icon in your Dock and select **Empty Trash**.
* **Clear the Photos "Recently Deleted" album:** Deleting photos doesn't instantly free up space. Open the **Photos** app, click **Recently Deleted** in the sidebar, and click **Delete All**.
* **Clean out your Downloads folder:** Open Finder > **Downloads**. Sort by **Size** and delete old disk images (`.dmg` or `.pkg` installers), zip files, and media files you no longer need.
* **Restart your Mac:** A restart clears out temporary virtual memory swap files (`/var/vm`) and system caches, which can instantly restore several gigabytes.

---

### 2. Use the Built-in Storage Manager

macOS has a built-in tool that shows what is taking up space:

1. Click the **Apple menu ()** > **System Settings** (or *About This Mac* on older macOS).
2. Go to **General** > **Storage**.
3. Review the categories:
   * **Documents:** Click the info icon (**ⓘ**). Use the **Large Files** and **File Browser** tabs to spot and delete huge files.
   * **Applications:** Sort by size and uninstall apps or games you no longer use (especially large games or unneeded software suites).
   * **macOS / iOS Backups:** If you back up your iPhone or iPad to your Mac, old backups can take 20–50+ GB. You can delete them directly from this screen.

---

### 3. Clear Hidden App Caches & Leftovers

Apps generate temporary cache files that macOS doesn't always automatically delete:

1. Open **Finder**.
2. Press `Command + Shift + G` to bring up the *Go to Folder* box.
3. Paste: `~/Library/Caches` and hit **Enter**.
4. Check for folders belonging to apps you recognize (e.g., browsers, Spotify, video editors) that have grown massive. You can safely delete the contents of these app cache folders.
5. Empty the Trash afterward.

*(Note: Delete the files **inside** the app's cache folder, rather than the entire `Library` directory).*

---

### 4. Fix High "System Data" (Local Snapshots)

If **System Data** is taking up 50–100+ GB, it is often due to **Time Machine local snapshots** (temporary backup snapshots saved to your internal drive when the backup drive isn't connected):

1. Open the **Terminal** app (via Spotlight / Command + Space).
2. Type this command to see existing snapshots and press Enter:
   ```bash
   tmutil listlocalsnapshots /
   ```
3. To delete them, run:
   ```bash
   tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 10000000000 4
   ```
   *(This tells macOS to aggressively purge local snapshots to free up space).*

---

### 5. Clear Developer Caches (If Applicable)

If you use your Mac for coding:
* **Xcode:** Open Finder > `Command + Shift + G` > go to `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData` and delete its contents.
* **Docker:** Run `docker system prune -a --volumes` in Terminal to clear unused containers and images.
* **Node.js:** Check for old projects packed with huge `node_modules` folders.

---

### 6. Visualize Large Files with a Free Tool

If you still can’t figure out where the space went, use a trusted, free visual disk analyzer to see exactly what folders are taking up gigabytes:
* **[OmniDiskSweeper](https://www.omnigroup.com/more)** (Free, lightweight; sorts every folder by size).
* **[GrandPerspective](https://grandperspectiv.sourceforge.net/)** (Free, open-source; displays a visual map of large files).

Most audio plug-ins on a Mac are installed in one of several standard folders, so removing them is usually a matter of deleting the right files. Quit your DAW first.

**1. Use the vendor's uninstaller if there is one**
Many developers ship an uninstaller, often in the installer package or in the plug-in's own folder. Use it when available because it removes all related files.

**2. Delete the plug-in files manually**
Plug-ins are typically found in these locations:

- **Audio Units (.component):** `/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components/` (system-wide) or `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components/` (current user only)
- **VST2 (.vst):** `/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST/` or `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST/`
- **VST3 (.vst3):** `/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/` or `~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/`
- **AAX (Pro Tools):** `/Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins/`
- **Some companion files** may also be in `/Library/Application Support/` under the developer's name, or in `~/Library/Application Support/`.

To open a folder: in Finder, press Command-Shift-G, paste the path, and press Return. Note that `/Library` is the system-wide folder and may require an administrator password. Move unwanted items to the Trash, then empty it.

**3. Clear the Audio Unit cache (optional)**
If an old Audio Unit still appears in Logic or GarageBand after you've deleted it, reset the cache. Quit your DAW, open Terminal, and run:

```
killall -9 AudioComponentRegistrar
```

Then restart your DAW. You can also check Logic's Plug-in Manager (Logic Pro > Settings > Plug-in Manager) to reset or disable plug-ins there.

**4. Check your DAW's plug-in list**
Some hosts, like Ableton Live or Reaper, have their own plug-in manager or scan settings. Rescan after removing files so stale entries disappear.

**Tips**
- If you're unsure whether a file is still needed, move it to a folder on your Desktop instead of deleting it, and check that your projects still open correctly before discarding it.
- Old projects that use a removed plug-in may show missing-plug-in warnings. Keep the installer if you might need it later.

To remove old audio plug-ins from your Mac, you generally delete their files from the specific folders where macOS stores them. 

Follow these steps:

---

### Step 1: Quit Your DAWs
Before deleting any files, completely close any digital audio workstation (DAW) you have open (Logic Pro, Ableton Live, FL Studio, Pro Tools, Reaper, etc.).

---

### Step 2: Delete Plugins from System Folders

Most audio plugins are stored in standard system folders. 

1. Open **Finder**.
2. Press **`Cmd + Shift + G`** (or go to **Go > Go to Folder...** in the top menu bar).
3. Paste the following path into the search bar and press **Return**:
   ```text
   /Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/
   ```
4. You will see several subfolders corresponding to different plugin formats:
   * **`Components/`** – Contains Audio Units (**AU**, used by Logic Pro, GarageBand, etc. Files end in `.component`).
   * **`VST/`** – Contains **VST2** plugins (Files end in `.vst`).
   * **`VST3/`** – Contains **VST3** plugins (Files end in `.vst3`).
   * **`CLAP/`** – Contains CLAP plugins (if you use this format).
5. Open the relevant folder(s), find the plugin(s) you no longer want, and move them to the **Trash**.

---

### Step 3: Check Avid / Pro Tools Plugins (AAX)
If you use Pro Tools, plugins are stored in a different location:

1. Press **`Cmd + Shift + G`** in Finder.
2. Go to:
   ```text
   /Library/Application Support/Avid/Audio/Plug-Ins/
   ```
3. Delete the `.aaxplugin` files for the plugins you want to remove.

---

### Step 4: Check the User Library (Less Common, but Possible)
Occasionally, plugins are installed only for your specific user account rather than system-wide:

1. Press **`Cmd + Shift + G`** in Finder.
2. Go to (note the `~` at the beginning):
   ```text
   ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/
   ```
3. Check the `Components`, `VST`, and `VST3` folders here as well and delete any old plugins.

---

### Step 5: Check Dedicated Brand Managers / Uninstallers
If the plugin belongs to a major developer suite, it is often better to use their official software to clean up accompanying samples, presets, and background services:

* **Waves:** Open **Waves Central** > *Uninstall*.
* **Native Instruments:** Open **Native Access** (or check their uninstaller apps).
* **Arturia:** Open **Arturia Software Center**.
* **Universal Audio:** Check the UAD uninstaller in `/Applications/Universal Audio/`.
* **iZotope:** Open **iZotope Product Portal**.

---

**System Data** is the catch-all category in macOS storage for files that don't fit anywhere else. Apple describes it as a general category for Apple and third-party files that don't belong to a more specific group ([Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102624)). Typical contents include caches, logs, temporary files, fonts, plug-ins, and app support files ([hometechops](https://hometechops.com/mac/mac-system-data-storage-huge)). It also commonly holds local Time Machine snapshots and old iPhone or iPad backups ([Setapp](https://setapp.com/how-to/macos-system-data-large)).

**You can't delete System Data as a whole.** It's a label for a group of files, not a folder, so you have to clear the things that make it up.

**How to shrink it, roughly from safest to most involved:**

1. **Restart your Mac.** Apps leave temporary files behind, and a reboot often clears many of them ([How-To Geek](https://www.howtogeek.com/why-is-system-data-taking-up-so-much-space-on-your-mac/)).
2. **Empty the Trash.** Files in the Trash still take up space until you permanently delete them ([Medium](https://medium.com/@zeng2483613716/why-system-data-is-huge-on-your-mac-and-how-i-actually-fix-it-381e299132db)).
3. **Remove leftover macOS installers.** After an update, the "Install macOS" app in Applications can take 12–15 GB, and it counts as System Data ([1dot.ai](https://1dot.ai/blog/how-to-reduce-system-data-on-mac)).
4. **Delete old iPhone/iPad backups.** Go to Finder, select your device, and remove old backups. Single backups can reach 20–40 GB ([Medium](https://medium.com/@zeng2483613716/why-system-data-is-huge-on-your-mac-and-how-i-actually-fix-it-381e299132db)).
5. **Thin Time Machine local snapshots.** These are temporary copies macOS keeps when your backup drive isn't connected. To see them, run `tmutil listlocalsnapshots /` in Terminal. To remove one, run `sudo tmutil deletelocalsnapshots TIMESTAMP`, replacing TIMESTAMP with the date from the list ([Medium](https://medium.com/@zeng2483613716/why-system-data-is-huge-on-your-mac-and-how-i-actually-fix-it-381e299132db)).
6. **Clear app caches.** Go to `~/Library/Caches` and remove the contents of individual app folders. Apps rebuild these as needed. Developer data like Xcode DerivedData and node_modules also often lands here ([1dot.ai](https://1dot.ai/blog/what-is-system-data-on-mac)).
7. **Turn on Optimize Storage.** Go to System Settings → General → Storage and enable it ([Tenorshare](https://www.tenorshare.com/mac-cleanup/how-to-clear-system-data-on-mac.html)).
8. **Uninstall unused apps and review big files.** Check the Applications and Documents categories using the More Info buttons in the Storage settings ([Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/en-us/102624)).

**Things to avoid:**
- Don't delete anything in the `/System` folder. Some of its contents are essential macOS files.
- Be cautious with third-party "cleaner" apps. They can purge data you actually need ([hometechops](https://hometechops.com/mac/mac-system-data-storage-huge)).
- Don't worry about a moderate amount. Around 12–25 GB is considered normal, and macOS frees space on its own when it needs to ([How-To Geek](https://www.howtogeek.com/why-is-system-data-taking-up-so-much-space-on-your-mac/)).

### What is “System Data” on Mac?

In macOS (found under **Apple menu  > System Settings > General > Storage**), **System Data** (formerly labeled **"Other"**) is a catch-all category for files that don’t fit neatly into specific buckets like Apps, Photos, Documents, or the core macOS operating system. 

It typically includes:
* **Caches and temporary files:** User cache, app cache, web browser cache, and system cache.
* **App Support files:** Data left behind by current and previously uninstalled applications (plugins, extensions, game assets, database files).
* **Time Machine local snapshots:** Incremental backups stored locally until your external drive is connected.
* **iOS / iPadOS backups:** Local backups created when syncing your iPhone/iPad to your Mac.
* **Developer tools and virtual machines:** Xcode derived data, simulator files, Docker containers/images, and virtual machine disks (Parallels, UTM).
* **Log files and crash reports.**

Because System Data isn’t a single file or app, **there is no single “Delete” button**. Instead, you have to clear out the specific files contributing to it.

---

### How to Delete and Reduce System Data

#### 1. Restart Your Mac
A simple restart triggers macOS’s built-in maintenance routines. It automatically purges temporary memory files, sleep image files, and system-level caches that might be temporarily counted toward System Data.

---

#### 2. Clear User and App Caches
Over time, caches from apps like Spotify, web browsers, and Adobe tools accumulate into dozens of gigabytes.

1. Open **Finder**.
2. Press **`Cmd + Shift + G`** (or select **Go > Go to Folder…** from the menu bar).
3. Type or paste:
   ```text
   ~/Library/Caches
   ```
   and press **Return**.
4. Inside, look for folders belonging to apps you recognize (or apps that use a lot of media). 
5. Select the files/folders inside them and move them to the **Trash**. *(Note: Do not delete the `Caches` folder itself, only items inside it. Your apps will rebuild these caches as needed).*
6. **Empty the Trash**.

---

#### 3. Remove Leftover App Support Files
When you drag an app to the Trash, its hidden support files often remain behind.

1. Press **`Cmd + Shift + G`** in Finder.
2. Enter:
   ```text
   ~/Library/Application Support
   ```
3. Look through the list for folders named after **apps you no longer use or already uninstalled**.
4. Move those abandoned folders to the Trash and empty it.

---

#### 4. Delete Time Machine Local Snapshots
If you use Time Machine, macOS saves backup snapshots to your internal drive when your backup disk isn't plugged in. These are flagged as "purgeable," but macOS counts them under System Data until space runs low.

To check and delete them:
1. Open the **Terminal** app (search via Spotlight with `Cmd + Space`).
2. Type the following command to list current snapshots:
   ```bash
   tmutil listlocalsnapshots /
   ```
3. If snapshots appear (e.g., `com.apple.TimeMachine.2024-05-10-153022`), delete one using:
   ```bash
   sudo tmutil deletelocalsnapshots 2024-05-10-153022
   ```
   *(Enter your Mac user password when prompted; typing will be hidden).*

---

#### 5. Delete Old iPhone / iPad Backups
Old device backups are often 10–50 GB each.

1. Go to **System Settings > General > Storage**.
2. Scroll to **iOS Files** (or **Device Backups**).
3. Click the **info (i)** icon next to it.
4. If old backups appear, select the outdated ones and click **Delete**.

---

#### 6. Clean Up Developer & VM Files (If Applicable)
If you do software development or run virtual machines, these frequently blow up System Data:
* **Xcode Derived Data:** Go to `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData` and delete the contents.
* **Docker:** Open Docker Desktop and purge unused images, containers, and volumes, or run `docker system prune -a` in Terminal.
* **Homebrew:** In Terminal, run `brew cleanup -s`.

---

#### 7. Find Hidden Space Hogs with a Disk Visualizer
If System Data is still unexpectedly large (e.g., 80 GB+) and you cannot find the source, the easiest way to locate it is with a free disk analyzer:
* **GrandPerspective** (Free, open-source)
* **OmniDiskSweeper** (Free)
* **DaisyDisk** (Free trial available)

These tools scan your entire drive and show you a visual breakdown of your files by size, making it obvious if a single app or hidden folder in `~/Library` is silently consuming 60 GB.

### 1. How They Handle Developer Caches

#### **CleanMyMac**
* **The Approach:** Automated scanning and categorization.
* **Xcode Support:** CleanMyMac has a dedicated **"Xcode Junk"** subcategory inside its *System Junk* module. It can automatically find:
  * `DerivedData`
  * Old iOS/watchOS/tvOS Device Support files (which can easily take 20–50 GB)
  * Xcode caches and old documentation
  * Unused Xcode archives
  * Old iOS Simulator runtimes
* **Non-Apple Development (Docker, Node, Python, Rust, etc.):** **Poor.** CleanMyMac has virtually no built-in awareness of deep dev environments. It does not scan for scattered `node_modules` folders, stale Docker virtual disks (`Docker.raw`), Cargo build artifacts (`target/`), or package manager caches (`~/.npm`, `~/.yarn`, `~/.cache/pip`).
* **Background Footprint:** Runs background monitoring daemons, menu bar widgets, and uses a subscription pricing model (or an expensive one-time license).

#### **DaisyDisk**
* **The Approach:** Interactive sunburst visualization of your entire filesystem.
* **Developer Cache Detection:** DaisyDisk has **no automated "Developer Cache" button**. Instead, it renders your disk graphically so you can spot massive hidden folders instantly. 
  * You will immediately see that `~/Library/Developer/` is eating 80 GB, or that Docker’s virtual disk (`~/Library/Containers/com.docker.docker/...`) is consuming 60 GB.
  * You can drill directly into `DerivedData` or project directories and drag them to the bottom-left "collector" to purge them.
* **Non-Apple Development:** Because it visually maps all data regardless of file type, it easily reveals bloated `target/` folders (Rust), `build/` directories, or `node_modules` clusters that automated cleaners ignore.
* **Background Footprint:** Extremely fast, zero background daemons, native macOS feel, and a low one-time purchase price.

### Important: How to Safely Clean Video Projects

Regardless of the tool you choose, deleting video files manually from the Finder level can corrupt your active project databases if done incorrectly:

1. **Final Cut Pro (FCP):** 
   * *Do not* dig inside the `.fcpbundle` package to delete files directly unless you are archiving. 
   * Instead, select your Library in FCP and go to **File > Delete Generated Library Files** to safely clear render files, proxies, and optimized media without touching your original media. Use DaisyDisk simply to locate which library has ballooned.
2. **Adobe Premiere Pro & After Effects:**
   * DaisyDisk is ideal for spotting the **Media Cache** and **Media Cache Files** folders (often hidden deep in `~/Library/Application Support/Adobe/Common`), as well as scratch disk preview folders, which can easily swallow hundreds of gigabytes.
3. **DaVinci Resolve:**
   * Use DaisyDisk to target your **`CacheClip`** and **`OptimizedMedia`** folders (defined in your Master Project Settings). These folders don't auto-purge and will quietly consume entire drives over time.
